findings.title: Hardcoded API Key in Source Code
findings.description: The VOICEVOX TTS API key is hardcoded directly in the source code as a string constant: `const API_KEY = "Q411563_2-i_70P";`. This key is committed to a public GitHub repository, meaning anyone can extract and abuse it. The key is used in every TTS request to the deprecatedapis.tts.quest service.
findings.recommendation: Move the API key to an environment variable (e.g., process.env.VOICEVOX_API_KEY) and load it via dotenv. The currently exposed key should be immediately rotated/revoked since it is publicly visible in the repository history.

findings.title: Hardcoded Discord User ID Leaked in Data Files
findings.description: The files dictionary.json and speakers.json both contain a hardcoded Discord user ID (1077177658758152253) committed to the public repository. This constitutes information disclosure of a real user's Discord identity tied to their speaker preferences.
findings.recommendation: Remove user-specific data from version-controlled files. Add dictionary.json and speakers.json to .gitignore (speakers.json is already partially gitignored as 'speaker.json' but the actual filename 'speakers.json' is NOT ignored). Initialize these files at runtime only if they do not exist.

findings.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) via User-Controlled Dictionary Regex
findings.description: The dictionary command allows any Discord user to add entries with `use_regex: true`. These user-supplied regex patterns are compiled with `new RegExp(entry.word, 'g')` in handleSpeak (src/handlers/vc/speak.ts, line 45) and applied to every message. A malicious user can craft a catastrophic backtracking regex pattern (e.g., `(a+)+$`) that causes the bot to hang indefinitely when processing messages, resulting in a Denial of Service.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) remove the regex option entirely and only allow literal string replacements, (2) validate regex patterns for safety using a library like 'safe-regex' or 're2', or (3) wrap regex execution in a timeout. Additionally, restrict dictionary management to users with specific Discord permissions (e.g., MANAGE_GUILD).

findings.title: No Permission Checks on Commands
findings.description: None of the slash commands (dictionary, join, leave, set-speaker) perform any permission checks. Any user in the server can: (1) modify the global dictionary with arbitrary regex patterns, (2) join/leave voice channels on behalf of the bot, (3) change speaker settings. The dictionary command is particularly dangerous as it allows persistent modification of bot behavior affecting all users.
findings.recommendation: Add permission checks using Discord's permission system. At minimum, restrict dictionary modifications to users with MANAGE_GUILD or a custom role. Consider using Discord's `default_member_permissions` field in command registration to restrict access.

findings.title: Excessive Discord Gateway Intents
findings.description: The bot requests ALL Discord gateway intents via `Object.values(GatewayIntentBits)`. This includes privileged intents such as GUILD_MEMBERS, GUILD_PRESENCES, and MESSAGE_CONTENT. The bot only needs GuildVoiceStates, GuildMessages, MessageContent, and Guilds. Requesting all intents violates the principle of least privilege and exposes the bot to unnecessary data, increasing the attack surface if the bot is compromised.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly specify only the required intents: [GatewayIntentBits.Guilds, GatewayIntentBits.GuildVoiceStates, GatewayIntentBits.GuildMessages, GatewayIntentBits.MessageContent].

findings.title: Unauthenticated Third-Party YouTube Download API Usage
findings.description: The youtube() method in voice.ts sends user-provided URLs to an unauthenticated third-party AWS Lambda endpoint (oo6o8y6la6.execute-api.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com) for YouTube downloading. This is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) risk: a malicious user could supply internal network URLs. Additionally, this third-party service is unverified and could return malicious content. The method also follows redirects to arbitrary URLs for audio fetching.
findings.recommendation: Validate that URLs are legitimate YouTube URLs before sending them to any processing service. Consider using an established, trusted library for YouTube audio extraction. Implement URL allowlisting to prevent SSRF. Note: this method appears unused currently but represents latent risk.

findings.title: User-Supplied Regex Can Cause Uncaught Exceptions
findings.description: When a user adds a dictionary entry with `use_regex: true` and provides an invalid regex pattern (e.g., `[invalid`), the `new RegExp(entry.word, 'g')` call in handleSpeak will throw a SyntaxError. While there is a try/catch in handleSpeak, invalid dictionary entries persist in the JSON file and will cause errors on every subsequent message until manually removed.
findings.recommendation: Validate the regex pattern at the time of dictionary addition (in the dictionary command handler) by wrapping `new RegExp(word)` in a try/catch. Reject invalid patterns before they are persisted to dictionary.json.

findings.title: Unvalidated Input Reflected in Discord Embeds
findings.description: User-supplied input (the 'word' and 'replacement' values from the dictionary command) is directly embedded into Discord embed descriptions using template literals with markdown bold formatting: `**${word}**`. While Discord's API escapes HTML, markdown injection could be used to create misleading messages (e.g., using markdown links, @everyone mentions in embeds, or excessively long strings).
findings.recommendation: Sanitize or escape user input before embedding it in Discord messages. Limit the length of word and replacement values. Strip or escape Discord markdown special characters.

findings.title: Sensitive Message Content Logged to Console
findings.description: The handleSpeak function logs the full content of every user message to the console: `console.log('Speak in ${message.channelId}: ${content}')`. This means all messages in monitored channels are written to server logs in plaintext, potentially including private or sensitive information shared by users.
findings.recommendation: Remove or minimize message content logging. If logging is needed for debugging, log only message metadata (channel ID, message ID, length) without the actual content. At minimum, truncate logged content to a few characters.

findings.title: Username Logged Without Sanitization
findings.description: The handleVcLogger handler logs usernames directly from Discord user objects to the console. While unlikely to be exploitable in a console context, if logs are ever displayed in a web dashboard or processed by log analysis tools, specially crafted usernames could lead to log injection or log forging attacks.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize usernames before logging by stripping or encoding control characters and newlines.

findings.title: Race Condition in File Write Operations
findings.description: The dictionary and set-speaker commands use synchronous fs.writeFileSync to persist data, but the in-memory sperkersData object is shared and mutated concurrently from multiple async command handlers without locking. If two users execute dictionary add commands simultaneously, the in-memory state and the file on disk may become inconsistent, potentially losing data.
findings.recommendation: Implement a mutex/lock around read-modify-write operations on sperkersData, or use an atomic file write approach (write to temp file, then rename).

findings.title: Gitignore Mismatch: speakers.json Not Actually Ignored
findings.description: The .gitignore file contains 'speaker.json' (singular) but the actual data file is 'speakers.json' (plural). As a result, speakers.json is tracked by git and committed to the public repository, exposing user Discord IDs and their speaker preferences.
findings.recommendation: Fix the .gitignore entry to 'speakers.json' (with the 's'). Remove the file from git tracking with `git rm --cached speakers.json`. Also add dictionary.json to .gitignore.

findings.title: Temporary Audio Files Not Securely Created
findings.description: The play() method creates temporary audio files in a predictable './temp' directory with timestamp-based filenames (`${Date.now()}.mp3`). This is predictable and could be subject to symlink attacks on shared systems. Additionally, the cleanup in the Idle event handler silently ignores errors (`fs.unlink(tempFilePath, () => {})`), potentially leaving orphaned temp files.
findings.recommendation: Use a cryptographically random filename (e.g., crypto.randomUUID()) for temp files. Use os.tmpdir() instead of a relative path. Implement periodic cleanup of old temp files to prevent disk exhaustion.

findings.title: No Input Length Validation on Dictionary Entries
findings.description: The dictionary command does not validate the length of 'word' or 'replacement' values. An attacker could add extremely long strings that consume memory and disk space, or add a large number of dictionary entries that slow down every message processing operation (each message iterates through all dictionary entries).
findings.recommendation: Add length limits for word and replacement values (e.g., max 100 characters each). Add a limit on the total number of dictionary entries (e.g., max 100 entries). Add rate limiting to prevent abuse.

findings.title: Deprecated TTS API Endpoint
findings.description: The bot uses `https://deprecatedapis.tts.quest/v2/voicevox/audio/` as the TTS endpoint. The domain name itself indicates this is a deprecated API, which may be discontinued at any time, potentially with no security updates or monitoring. Using deprecated APIs increases risk of supply-chain compromise if the domain is abandoned and re-registered by a malicious actor.
findings.recommendation: Migrate to a supported, actively maintained TTS API. If self-hosting is feasible, run a local VOICEVOX engine instance to eliminate third-party API dependency entirely.

findings.title: No Rate Limiting on TTS Requests
findings.description: Every message in a monitored channel triggers a TTS API call with no rate limiting. A user could spam messages to exhaust the TTS API quota, cause excessive network traffic, or incur API costs. The bot only checks if audio is currently playing and queues the next message, but does not limit the rate of API calls.
findings.recommendation: Implement rate limiting per user and per channel. Add a maximum queue size for pending TTS requests. Consider adding a cooldown period between messages from the same user.

findings.title: Error Details Potentially Leaked to Users
findings.description: The logAndSendError function in index.ts logs full error objects to the console including stack traces. While the error message sent to Discord users is generic ('There was an error while executing this interaction!'), the console output could contain sensitive internal details if logs are accessible.
findings.recommendation: Ensure server logs are properly secured and not accessible to unauthorized parties. Consider structured logging with appropriate log levels.

findings.title: Spoofed User-Agent Headers in HTTP Requests
findings.description: Multiple fetch() calls in voice.ts use a hardcoded Chrome User-Agent string to impersonate a browser. This is a deceptive practice that may violate the terms of service of the APIs being called and could mask the bot's true identity in server logs.
findings.recommendation: Use an honest User-Agent string that identifies the bot (e.g., 'Nanase-Speaker-Bot/0.0.1'). If the API requires a browser User-Agent, document why this is necessary.
